Satisfaction with adult children's achievements is associated with depression and loneliness in later-life: the mediating roles of children's support and gratitude
Babatola Dominic Olawaa and Erhabor Sunday Idemudiaa
a Lifestyle and Disease Research Entity, North-West University, Marfikeng, South Africa

We examined the mediating roles of gratitude and children support in the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements, and depression/loneliness in a sample of 465 community elders of Ekiti State, Nigeria. The sample includes 294 women and 171 men with mean age 74.18 (SD = 9.42) selected by means of multistage sampling method. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM). Results suggested that satisfaction with adult children's achievements was negatively associated with depression and loneliness. However, these relationships were found to be successively mediated by children's support and gratitude. Specifically, gratitude fully mediated the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness while children's support was a partial mediator. Also, gratitude partially mediated the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression while children's support did not. The fit indices for the mediation model achieved the acceptable cuff-off for model fitness, CFI = .95, RMSEA = .042, 90% CI = (.033, .05, SRMR = .05, with 46% and 28% variance in depression and loneliness, respectively. In the management of geriatric depression and loneliness, mental health professionals may assess satisfaction with adult children's achievements and utilize gratitude interventions for a happy and successful aging.

Depression is considered the most common mental disorder in old age (Babatsikou, Konsolaki, Kouri, Zyga, & Koutis, 2017) and foremost in the cause of disease burden and disability world-wide (Wang, Hu, Xiao, & Zhou, 2017). It is a debilitating illness that makes the sufferer experience intense sadness, negative self-worth, guilty feelings, impaired sleep and lack of pleasure from life, hopelessness, helplessness and suicidal thoughts (National Health Service, 2016). The global prevalence of geriatric depression is estimated at 7% (World Health Organization, 2017) but could be as high as 40% among older adults in nursing homes/clinic settings (Padayacheya, Ramlalla, & Chipp, 2017; Royal College of Psychiatrists & British Geriatric Society, 2018) and more than 30% in the general population of some particular countries including Nigeria (e.g. Awunor et al., 2018; Dao, Nguyen, Nguyen, & Nguyen, 2018; Mirkena, Reta, Haile, Nassir, & Sisay, 2018). Unmanaged depression could have detrimental consequences for older people. Niles and O'Donovan (2019) demonstrated that unmanaged geriatric depression is a strong predictor of increased incidence of medical illness (e.g. heart disease, stroke, diabetes) and somatic symptoms (e.g. shortness of breath, dizziness, back pain, visual impairments). Independent of the effects of cardiovascular diseases, new findings showed that depression increases the risk of earlier mortality among older adults (Péquignot et al., 2019).

Unfortunately, it is established that older adults are less likely to include depression among presenting problems during medical visits, given the idea that depression is a normal part of the aging process (Snowden & Steinman, 2017; Weber, 2015).

Further, studies have shown that loneliness and depression co-occur in old age (e.g. Bath, Yang, & Nicholls, 2018; Courtin & Knapp, 2017; Domènech-Abella et al., 2017) and that geriatric loneliness in particular, continue to be a public health issue in these present times (Mental Health Foundation. & Age Scotland, 2017). Loneliness is described as an unpleasant internal subjective state that occurs when there is decline in one's social networks both quantitatively and qualitatively (Chana, Marshall, & Harley, 2016; Chen, Dattilo, & Frias, 2018). Reduction in social networks increases the vulnerability of older adults to both social and emotional loneliness (Ogundiran, 2017; Utz, Swenson, Caserta, Lund, & DeVries, 2014). Social loneliness is the loss of a wider circle of friends, family and acquaintances required for enablement of companionship feelings and communal life, whereas emotional loneliness is the loss of an attachment figure(s) which one looks up to for provision of deeper emotional support (Dahlberg & McKee, 2014). Thus, while decrease in quantity of social networks may make one vulnerable to experiencing social loneliness, decline in quality social networks may lead to emotional loneliness. The prevalence of loneliness could range between 8.6 and 70% (Dahlberga, Agahia, & Lennartssona, 2018; Vozikaki, Papadaki, Linardakis, & Philalithis, 2018; Dahlberg & McKee, 2014, Yang & Gu, 2019; Hansen & Slagsvold, 2015; Nzabona, Ntozi, & Rutaremwa, 2016). Loneliness is well established to predict depression and psychological distress (Dahlberga et al., 2018; Ng & Lee, 2019), cognitive deficits (Donovan et al., 2016), malnutrition (Eskelinen, Hartikainen, & Nykanen, 2016), physical health decline (Singer, 2018) and premature mortality (Cacioppo & Cacioppo, 2018) among older adults.

Past studies have evidenced the predictors of depression and loneliness among older adults. These are inclusive, but not exhaustive of physical health burdens, self-rated heath and stress (Gonyea, Curley, Melekis, Levine, & Lee, 2018; Olawa, Adebayo, Mokuolu, Umeh, & Omolayo, 2018; Richard et al., 2017; Yang & Bath, 2018), widowhood and mobility problems (Dahlberg, Andersson, McKee, & Lennartsson, 2015; Padayacheya et al., 2017; Yang & Bath, 2018), size and type of social network (Domènech-Abella et al., 2017; Faronbi et al., 2017) and financial strains (Cohen-Mansfield, Hazan, Lerman, & Shalom, 2016; Wilkinson, 2016).

However, further research is needed to demonstrate the role played by satisfaction with adult children's achievements on later life depression and loneliness given that children's successes and failures may influence mental health at old age (Fingerman, Miller, Birditt, & Zarit, 2009). Beginning from conception, parents devote time and effort in the nurturing process by investing considerable amount of physical, social and emotion resources on children for attainment of adult milestones which are typically expected in areas of education, career, finances, health, social and emotional adjustments (Birditta, Kim, Zaritc, Fingerman, & Loving, 2016; Campbell et al., 2012). However, it is shown that while some children become successful adults and provide fulfilments for parents, others become unsuccessful and constitute sources of serious problems (Cichy, Lefkowitz, Davis, & Fingerman, 2013; Birditt, Fingerman, & Zarit, 2010). Children with lower levels of achievements in career and relationships evoke parental anger, worry, disappointments and guilt (Cichy, Lefkowitz, Davis, & Fingerman, 2013). There is also evidence that adult children's higher socioeconomic status and successful marital life predict less ambivalence in older parents while the need to provide monetary support to adult children was associated with greater parental ambivalence (Guo, 2009; Kiecolt, Blieszner, & Savla, 2011). Also, older parents experience severe distress when adult children suffer for serious mental illness (Barker, Greenberg, Seltzer, & Almeida, 2012).

Based on the established relationship between children successes/failure and parental distress, it is hypothesized in the present study that parental satisfaction with adult children's achievements will be related to geriatric depression and loneliness. However, these relationships are assumed to be mediated by feelings of gratitude and perception of support from children. In other words, when parents are satisfied with the achievements of their adult children, it is presumed that they would express gratitude/thankfulness and report increased perception of support from children, thus

predicting lower loneliness feelings and depression. These associations are grounded on findings that elderly satisfaction with life events is positively related to expression of gratitude (e.g. Robustelli & Whisman, 2018; Yildirim & Alanazi, 2018) and expression of gratitude is related to lower levels of depression (e.g. Zhang, Mou, Tong & Wu, 2018; Petrocchi & Couyoumdjian, 2015) and loneliness (e.g. Caputo, 2015; O'Connell, O'Shea, & Gallagher, 2016). Similarly, satisfaction with life events is shown to be positively related to family support- inclusive of children (e.g. Bai, Yang, & Knapp, 2018; Jaradat & Abood, 2016), and adult children support is associated with lower depression (e.g. Djundeva, Mills, Wittek, & Steverink, 2015; Li, Ji, & Chen, 2014) and decreased loneliness (Rodriguez, Gierveld, & Buz, 2014; Teh, Tey, & Ng, 2014).

The outcome of the this work will inform us of the possible relationship between parents' satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness/depression, and the potential mediating influences of gratitude feelings and children's supports. This will help mental health professionals manage geriatric depression and loneliness from satisfaction with children's achievements through gratitude and children support.

Participants include 465 older adults (comprising of 294 women) drawn from the three senatorial districts of Ekiti State, Nigeria by means of multistage sampling technique. The mean age of sample was 74.18 years (± 9.42) with age range 60–96 years. Sample size was determined by using the Yamane's (1967) procedure with a precision value of .05 and estimated Ekiti State elderly population of 137,415 (National Population Commission, (2009) . The multistage process involved a simple random selection of two local government areas (LGAs) from each of the three senatorial districts of Ekiti State, thus totaling six LGAs. Further, three communities were randomly selected from each of the six LGAs with the exception of two LGAs where one community was individually chosen due to the fact that they were one-community LGA. In all, data were collected from 14 community settings covering the three senatorial districts. Sample was almost equal for all the districts which include Ekiti North (n = 169), Ekiti Central (n = 149) and Ekiti South (n = 147).

We began data collection with the help of five trained research assistants after the study was ethically approved by the Institutional Review Board. Upon arrival at selected communities, the initial task was to get authorization to conduct the study from individual community heads. Following the authorizations, we numbered the streets within each community according to their topography and selected only streets that were odd numbered. Within selected streets, participants were recruited for interview via home-home contacts after obtaining either verbal or written informed consents. Inclusion criteria were being 60 years and over, ability to speak and understand either Yoruba or English Language, with no sign of cognitive disorientation and hearing impairments. All these were determined during an initial rapport with participants. We obtained a response rate of 97%.

Depression. Depression was measured using the 5-item geriatric depression scale (GDS). The 5-item GDS was designed to assess depression in community, nursing homes and hospitalized older adults, and shown to be as effective as the 15-item GDS (Rinaldi et al., 2003). It is scored on a "Yes (1) or No (0)" response format with item 1 reversed coded. "In examining its validity, the 5-item GDS and the 15-item GDS showed a significant agreement with the clinical diagnosis of depression (k = 0.74 for both scales). The 5-item GDS had good inter-rater reliability (k = 0.88) and test–retest reliability (k = 0.84)" (Rinaldi et al., 2003, p. 295). Pilot testing results (using a sample size of 63 older adults from Ado-Ekiti) showed that the 5-item GDS correlates positively (r = .43) with scores on the

Geriatric Anxiety Inventory-Short Form (Byrne & Pachana, 2010) and has 2-week test–retest reliability coefficient of .90. However, in structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis items 4 and 5 of the GDS were deleted because of non-significant factor loadings less than .10.

Loneliness. Loneliness was assessed by means of the 3-item loneliness scale (Hughes, Waite, Hawkley, & Cacioppo, 2004). The 3-item loneliness scale was constructed by extracting items from the R-UCLA Loneliness Scale (Russell, Peplau, & Cutrona, 1980). The items are scored on a 3-point Likert scale format which are 1 (hardly ever), 2 (some of the time), and 3 (often). Adequate validity and reliability coefficients are evidenced for the 3-item loneliness scale (Hughes et al., 2004). Scores on the 3-item loneliness scale was found to be positively correlated with scores on the geriatric anxiety inventory – short form (r = .41) and 5-item geriatric depression scale (r = .32) during pilot testing. The scale also has an acceptable internal consistency coefficient of .81.

Satisfaction with adult children's achievements. This was measured by asking participants to generally express their level of satisfaction with adult children's achievements in six areas namely education, occupation, health, finances, relationships and closeness to God using a 5-point Likert scale format which are as follows: very dissatisfied (0), dissatisfied (1), neither satisfied nor dissatisfied (2), satisfy (3) and very satisfied (4). Responses were based on the general satisfaction with the achievements of all adult children taken together and not just a particular adult child. Parents were asked to limit their ratings to adult children who have attained at least the age of 25. At this age, it is maximally possible (under normal circumstances) that an adult child would have attained a first degree education, have a job and developed mature relationships with the opposite sex whether marital or not. These assumptions were based on the evidence that the minimum age required for a child to gain admission into Nigerian higher institutions is 16 years (Lawal, 2018). Hence by age 20 (without any obstruction), adult children would have completed a first-degree education and ready to go into the world of work. An internal consistency coefficient of .75 was obtained for the measure of satisfaction with adult children's achievements. Also, present study data fits the underlying construct of satisfaction with adult children achievements, χ2 (5) = 9.21, p = .10, CF1 = .99, SRMR = .02, RMSEA = .043, and 90% CI = (.00, .085).

Gratitude. This was measured using Gratitude Questionnaire (GQ-6). GQ-6 is a short, self-report instrument developed to assess the feelings or disposition to experience gratitude or express thankfulness (McCullough, Emmons & Tsang, 2002). Responses were measured on a 7-point Likert scale format ranging from "strongly disagree" (1) to "strongly agree" (7). The internal reliability coefficient of the scale as reported by authors is between alphas .82 and .87 (McCullough, Emmons & Tsang, 2002). The GQ-6 has been shown to be a valid measure. It is positively correlated with scores on optimism, life satisfaction, hope, spirituality and religiousness, forgiveness, empathy and prosocial behavior, and negatively related to depression, anxiety, materialism and envy (Jarden, 2011). An internal consistency coefficient of .71 was obtained for the GQ-6 during pilot testing and a convergent validity coefficient of .33 with scores on the Daily Spiritual Experience Scale (DSES). In addition, the gratitude construct fits the data of the present study, χ2 (5) = 6.3, p = .28, CF1 = .99, SRMR = .02, RMSEA = .02, and 90% CI = (.00, .072). However, item 6 was deleted in SEM analysis because of non-significant factor loading of .04.

children's support. This was assessed by a single-item measure of children support in the Duke Social Support and Stress Scale (DUSOCS; Parkerson et al., 1989) by asking older adults the level of support they presently receive from children or grandchildren. Response includes "none (0), some (1), a lot (2), there is no such person (0)." In examining the validity of a single-item measure of children support to parents, we correlated the individual item scores on the Duke Social Support

subscale with the aggregate score on satisfaction with children achievements during pilot testing. Outcomes showed that the correlations coefficient between satisfaction with adult children achievements (SACA) and children support (r = .56, p < .001) was higher than the coefficients between SACA and wife/husband/significant other support (r = .31, p = .027); SACA and relatives by marriage support (r = .38, p = .007). However, satisfaction with adult children's achievements was not related with scores on the other items of the Duke Social Support subscale specifying support from parents or grandparents, brothers or sisters, other blood relatives, neighbors, co-workers, church/mosque members and other friends. These demonstrate potential convergent and discriminant validity for the single-item measure of children support to parents.

Following the International Test Commission (2010) procedures, we adapted and translated study instruments from English to Yoruba language using both judgmental (backward translation) and statistical (correlation of the test scores on both languages as answered by bilingual respondents) designs to accommodate older adults who are not proficient in the use of English language. Test– retest correlation between source and target language of research instruments range from .64 to .95.

Independent sample t-test and one-way ANOVA were used to analyze differences of sociodemographic variables on depression and loneliness through IBM SPSS software (Version 20.0). Bivariate relationships among study variables were tested using Pearson's (r). We used SEM with maximum likelihood to estimate both direct and indirect paths between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression/loneliness. SEM was calculated with the aid of IBM SPSS AMOS (version 25.0).

All study variables except children's support and demographic variables were constructed as latent variables to avoid biased estimation due to measurement error (Kline, 2011). We examined normality of data by calculating the skewness scores of observed variable and indicators of all latent variables. Data were considered as deviating from moderate normality if skewness scores fall outside the range of −1 to 1 (Blanca, Arnau, L_opez-Montiel, Bono, & Bendayan, 2013). To achieve normality, we reflected and inversed scores that showed severe negative skewedness, and log10 transformation for substantial positively skewed scores (Mertler & Vannatta, 2005). There was no outlier in data distribution as z scores for all cases were within −4 to +4 (Stevens, 1992). Missing scores were replaced with the mean values in affected cases given that missing scores were not more than 15% of cases (Hair, Black, Babin, & Anderson, 2010). We used the standardized root-meansquare residual (SRMR), comparative fit index (CFI) and root-mean-square of approximation (RMSEA) to examine model fitness. An adequate fit is obtained if the SRMR and RMSEA are below .06 and .08, respectively, and CFI value above .90 (Kline, 2011).

We initially examined a model predicting depression and loneliness from satisfaction with adult children's achievements without the mediating variables. Results indicated that the paths from satisfaction with adult children's achievements to depression [β = −.54, p < .001] and loneliness [β = −.23, p < .001] were both significant with 30% and 5% variance, respectively. The fit indices for the model met the acceptable criteria for model fitness, CFI = .95, RMSEA = .05, 90% CI = (.038, .065), SRMR = .05. In a preliminary mediation model, we specified sex, widowhood, education, occupation and family type as control variables given that they significantly influenced depression and/loneliness as indicated in Table 1. Analyses outcomes showed that sex [β = −.02, p = .68], education [β = −.06, p = .20], family type [β = −.07, p = .15] and occupation [β = −.07, p = .20] did not significantly predict loneliness. Also, widowhood [β = .14, p = .08] and occupation [β = −.07, p = .37] were found not to predict depression. However, widowhood significantly predicted loneliness [β = .29, p < .001]. Hence, only widowhood was included in the final mediation model as control variable.

Figure 1 displays the standardized estimates for the final model. Factor loadings of the indicators of satisfaction with adult children's achievements, gratitude, depression and loneliness were all significant. The fit indices for the model achieved the acceptable cuff-off for model fit, CFI = .95, RMSEA = .042, 90% CI = (.033, .05, SRMR = .05, with 46% and 28% variance in depression and loneliness, respectively. The paths from satisfaction with adult children's achievements to gratitude [β = .33, p < .001] and children support [β = .42, p < .001] were significant. The path from gratitude to depression [β = −.388, p < .001] and loneliness [β = −.389, p < .001] were also significant. While the path from children support to loneliness was significant [β = −.15, p = .006], the part from children support to depression was not [β = −.07, p = .45]. Further, the path from children support to gratitude was found to be significant [β = .22, p < .001]. Additionally, result showed that the direct effect of satisfaction with adult children's achievements on depression was significant [β = −.38, p = .002], whereas the direct effect of satisfaction with adult children's achievements on loneliness became non-significant [β = .002, p = .97].

Mediation evidence in an SEM framework demands that both total effects and indirect effects be significant (Preacher & Hayes, 2004). The total effects of satisfaction with adult children's achievements on depression [β = −.144, p = .008] and loneliness [β = −.137, p = .007] were significant. Total indirect effects of satisfaction with adult children's achievements on depression [β = −.20, p = .014] and loneliness [β = −.23, p = .005] were also significant. Specific indirect effects were calculated using bootstrapping. Table 3 shows 90% and 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals for specific indirect effects.

Except for the specific indirect effect of the path from satisfaction with adult children's achievements through children's support to depression, all specific indirect effects did not pass through zero, indicating significant specific indirect effects for these paths. These indicate that gratitude significantly mediates the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression [β = −.032, p = .001]/loneliness [β = −.073, p = .001]. Children's support mediates the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness [β = −.034, p = .018] but not depression [β = −.003, p = .759]. In addition, the relationships between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression [β = −.009, p = .002]/loneliness [β = −.022, p = .002] were significantly and successively mediated through children support and then gratitude.

Given that the direct effect of satisfaction with adult children's achievements to loneliness was not significant in the mediation model, it was necessary to test whether this came about through gratitude or children's support or successively through children support and then gratitude. Specifying gratitude as the only mediator between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness generated a non-significant direct effect [β = −.09, p = .15]. Also, specifying only the paths successively passing through children's support and gratitude as mediators produced a non-significant beta weight [β = −.05, p = .41]. Although it is known that achievements of adult children are linked with psychological health of older parents (Cichy et al., 2013), research literature is yet to specifically demonstrate whether expression of satisfaction with these achievements are related to depression and loneliness in laterlife. In this regard, the present study investigated the associations between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and geriatric depression/loneliness and the possible mediating roles of support from children and feelings of gratitude.

Results of SEM analysis confirmed that satisfaction with adult children's achievements significantly predicted both geriatric depression and loneliness with stronger beta weight and variance for depression, which implies that satisfaction with adult children's achievements may be more influential on depression than loneliness. Specifically, increase in satisfaction with adult children's achievements predicts less depressive and loneliness feelings. When elderly individuals are satisfied with adult children's achievements, they are likely to feel the sense of accomplishments that efforts expended on the rearing process were not futile after all. This sense of accomplishments possibly increases happiness levels and reduces depressive and loneliness feelings. On the other hand, lower satisfaction with adult children's achievements may make older adults develop sense of parenthood failures and regret (Fingerman, Cheng, Birditt, & Zarit, 2012; Pillemer, Suitor, Mueller-Johnson, Sechrist, & Heidorn, 2006).

Further, results showed that satisfaction with adult children's achievements predicted gratitude. In particular, an increase in satisfaction predict increase in gratitude feelings. This suggests that satisfaction with achievements of adult children enables feelings of thankfulness. Results confirmed previous findings that showed that satisfaction with life events in later-life predispose feelings of gratitude (Robustelli & Whisman, 2018; Yildirim & Alanazi, 2018). Also, findings demonstrate that being satisfied with adult children's achievements predicts perception of children's support. This indicates that the more parents are satisfied with the achievements of children the more they are likely to perceive reception of support from them. Outcomes somehow give credence to past studies that showed that satisfaction with life events is related to family support which is inclusive of children (Bai et al., 2018; Jaradat & Abood, 2016).

By confirming the outcomes of previous works (O'Connell et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018), results also suggest that increased in gratitude feelings predicted lower levels of depression and loneliness. This is expected given that gratitude creates sense of thankfulness even for the smallest favors received and provide valuable coping skills for dealing with stress and losses (Emmons & Mishra, 2011). Elderly individuals with gratitude orientation, may not be depressed because they focus on gains acquired prior to the onset of their difficulties. The predictive ability of gratitude on loneliness may be theoretically accounted for by the find-remind-and- bind model of gratitude (Algoe, 2012). According to this model, gratitude functions by helping the fortification of social bonds and strengthening of existing interpersonal relationships (O'Connell et al., 2016). In other words, being thankful inclines grateful people to readily appreciate and return kindness toward others, and reciprocally, others show benevolence toward them. This cycle of showering of kindness enables the maintenance of existing and new social connections needed to counteract loneliness (Lim, Gleeson, Jackson, & Fernandez, 2014).

Moreover, results showed that perception of support from children predicted depression and loneliness. Increased perception of children's support predicted lower feelings of depression and loneliness. These findings support previous works that demonstrated the protective role of family support on loneliness (e.g. Teh et al., 2014) and depression (e.g. Djundeva et al., 2015). In later-life, supports from children may provide older adults the opportunity of maintaining social connections with their offspring, and meeting of daily financial and economic needs, which in turn, may have mitigating effects on loneliness and depression.

Outcomes of mediation analysis showed that gratitude mediates the influence of satisfaction with adult children's achievements on both depression and loneliness while children's support only mediates the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression. While children's support partially mediates the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness, gratitude was found to be a perfect mediator. In addition, children's support and gratitude partly and successively mediate the influence of satisfaction with adult children's achievements on depression. However, there was a full successive mediation of children's support and gratitude in the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness.

The implications of mediation findings are in four folds. First, satisfaction of parents with children achievements relieves older adults from loneliness necessarily through gratitude. In other words, satisfaction with children achievements enables feelings of gratitude, which in turn, perfectly reduce loneliness feelings. If parents do not feel grateful for the satisfaction experienced from children achievements, they may not experience full reduction in loneliness given that gratitude is a necessary link between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness. Second, children's support partly explains why satisfaction with adult children's achievements influences loneliness. It is implied that when older adults are satisfied with children's achievement, they are more likely to perceive support from children, and then feel relatively less lonely. Third, gratitude partly explains the link between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression. This suggests that when older adults are satisfied with children's achievements, they feel grateful and then partly feel less depressed. Fourth, satisfaction with adult children's achievements is directly linked with depression without support from children. In this sense, the satisfaction derived from achievements of children can in itself lower geriatric depression without reception of support from children. However, result showed that children's support may mediate the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression through gratitude.

The current study is not without limitations. Drawing causal relationships between variables may be limited since our data was a cross-sectional one. Longitudinal data are needed to confirm findings in order to draw cause-effect relationships among variables. Quality of findings may be challenged given that we used only the questionnaire method for data collection. This limitation may have resulted into social desirability responding. However, limitation is minimized through the use of reliable and validated set of instruments. Also, ratings of satisfaction with adult children's achievements were based on the overall assessment of satisfaction with achievements of all adult children per participant and not specifically for every adult child. As a result, individual participants might have in a bias manner reported level of satisfaction by rating the achievements of all adult children together. A more objective approach would have been an independent assessment of satisfaction with the achievements of every adult child. Also, our sample consists of mostly women and less educated older adults thereby limiting the generalizability of study findings to men and well educated elderly individuals. Nevertheless, we controlled for these differences in preliminary SEM analysis and found that they may not actually confound results. Future studies may consider a more representative sample.

Notwithstanding these limitations, the findings have empirically demonstrated that satisfaction with adult children's achievements is a significant predictor of depression and loneliness in later life. In addition, gratitude and children's supports successively mediated the relationship between satisfaction

with adult children's achievements and depression/loneliness. Specifically, gratitude fully mediated the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and loneliness while children support was a partial mediator. Moreover, gratitude partially mediated the relationship between satisfaction with adult children's achievements and depression while children's support did not. In the management of geriatric depression and loneliness, mental health professionals may assess older adults' satisfaction with adult children's achievements and utilize gratitude interventions for a happy and successful aging.
